To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) platelets and immune cells are key players of tissue healing; (ii) platelet-rich plasma (PRP) can be used to promote tissue repair and regeneration, and (iii) PRP and/or immune cell-derived factors can be used to activate endogenous stem cells to repair tissue lesions.

the use of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and/or platelet-rich fibrin (PRF), alone or associated with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and/or growth factors, can be used to boost endogenous regeneration in critical or difficult-to-heals wounds, and to enhance the efficacy of cell therapy and/or tissue engineering approaches.
the activation of innate immunity and the recruitment of immune cells to a wound site can be used as an innovative tool to promote the endogenous repair of large tissue defects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying and developing innovative tools to boost endogenous repair of critical or difficult-to-healing large tissue defects.

the identification and characterization of innovative tools, such as platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and immune cells, that can be applied to promote endogenous regeneration in chronic or difficult-to-treat tissue lesions and defects.

the identification of novel tools that could be used in the future to promote endogenous regeneration of chronic or difficult-treat wounds, such as diabetic foot ulcers, venous ulcers, and pressure ulcers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a combination of platelet-rich plasma and mesenchymal stem cells is a promising strategy for regenerative medicine, particularly for the treatment of chronic or difficult to heal tissue defects.

, to date, the most effective strategy to repair large tissue defects is to use the patient’s own stem/progenitor and differentiated cells, which are activated by a local microenvironment that is reconstituted by the administration of a combination of factors, such as cytokines, growth factors, and extracellular matrix proteins.
the development of new tools inspired from nature, to be used alone or associated to “ex vivo” cell therapy, will be the future of regenerative medicine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of “exogenous” platelets, or of their secreted products, in combination with immune cells and/or stem/progenitor cell populations, can reactivate endogenous tissue repair mechanisms and boost the regeneration of large tissue lesions.
, by combining the knowledge of tissue biology and regenerative medicine, it is possible to develop new regimens for the treatment of large and difficult-to-heal wounds.

the combination of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) with immune cells (e.g., monocytes/macrophages) or their soluble products (e.g., cytokines) could be a promising strategy to promote endogenous repair of chronic wounds, large bone defects, and critical ischemia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the activation of the innate immune response, by the use of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) or other platelet concentrates, can reactivate endogenous tissue repair and regeneration mechanisms.

, by mimicking the physiological tissue healing mechanisms, we can boost the intrinsic tissue repair mechanisms, and thus, we can achieve tissue repair without the need for exogenous stem/progenitor cell delivery.

the use of a single or a combination of the following strategies: 1. platelet concentrates (PCs), 2. mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs), 3. platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and 4. granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), could be used to reactivate endogenous repair mechanisms in patients with critical tissue lesions and defects.
